book.title: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing
book.author: John C. Bogle

confidence_note: The 12.5% vs 7.3% figures for 1980-2005 come from one secondary article summarising Bogle's chapter 'The Grand Illusion'; the share of the gap due to costs is stated vaguely there, so only 'part' is used. The old text's 'best 30 days' statistic could not be tied to Bogle and was dropped. The dollar illustration is the writer's own compounding of the two rates and must be labelled as arithmetic.
facts: In the chapter 'The Grand Illusion' Bogle compares 25 years, 1980 to 2005.
The average fund investor earned 7.3% a year.
Costs explain only part of the gap; the main cause is investor behaviour, especially timing and fund selection.
Investors tend to buy funds after they have done well and sell after they have done poorly.
Writer's arithmetic, not Bogle's figure: as steady yearly rates over 25 years, $10,000 would reach about $190,000 at 12.5% and about $58,000 at 7.3%.
A separate Dalbar survey (20 years to Dec 31, 2010): stock fund investors 3.83% a year vs 9.14% for the S&P 500; not Bogle's figures.
scene_details: 12.5% a year for the index over 25 years
7.3% a year for the average fund investor
buying a fund after a strong stretch, selling after a weak one
tension: The index and the people who own funds in it do not get the same return.
opening_idea: Open with the two numbers over the same 25 years.

lessons.idea: Your own buying and selling decides your return as much as the product you hold.
lessons.anchor: 12.5% for the index and 7.3% for the average investor.

reflect_final: Think of the last time you changed a money plan after a recent result; what had actually changed apart from the number you were looking at?

use_cases.situation: A friend wants to move into whatever fund did best last year
use_cases.move: Say: Bogle found the average fund investor earned 7.3% when the index made 12.5%. Let's write down why we would switch.

use_cases.situation: Markets fall and you feel like selling
use_cases.move: Wait one day and write down what changed in your plan, not in the price.

use_cases.situation: A couple reviewing their joint investments
use_cases.move: Agree on one rule for when you will buy or sell, before the next news cycle.

pocket_idea: Over 25 years the index paid 12.5% a year and the average fund investor kept 7.3%: the gap came largely from when and what people bought.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Over the same 25 years the index made 12.5% a year and the average fund investor 7.3%.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Bogle compares 1980 to 2005: S&P 500 12.5% a year, average fund investor 7.3%; the gap is mostly timing and fund choice, buying after gains and selling after losses.
